chunks.text:
French philosopher whose work explores multiplicity, becoming, and the creation of concepts. These notes concern his reading of Nietzsche.

## forces.

See also: [action theory](/thoughts/action-theory) and [Nietzsche](/thoughts/Philosophy-and-Nietzsche).

In [Nietzsche and Philosophy](/library/Nietzsche-and-Philosophy), Deleuze treats [will to power](/thoughts/Will-to-Power) as the principle determining relations between forces. Calling it another force obscures that distinction. A [desire](/thoughts/desire) for domination already presupposes a valuation of power.[^3]

Active and reactive name qualities of forces: active forces create forms and directions, while reactive forces conserve and adapt. Affirmation and negation name qualities of the [will](/thoughts/Will) to power. These pairs are related and must be kept distinct.[^3]

In his reading of Nietzsche's [genealogy of morals](/library/On-The-Genealogy-of-Morals), overcoming nihilism requires a change in how values are produced. Negation becomes subordinate to affirmation; opposition to existing values alone leaves that source of evaluation unexamined.[^3]

His account of multiplicity asks how something acquires consistency while its relations change. Tampio distinguishes countable multiplicities from qualitative ones, such as a changing mood. The two can coexist in the same experience.[^1]

Deleuze reads the dice throw as an affirmation of becoming. Throwing affirms chance, including its multiplicity and [chaos](/thoughts/Chaos); the combination formed when the dice land affirms necessity. Both moments belong to the same throw. This is his philosophical reading of eternal return.[^2][^3]

[^3]: Gilles Deleuze, [Nietzsche and Philosophy](https://on-air.caricomassimo.org/media/pages/airchive/nietzsche-and-philosophy/7c243c2804-1715897949/gilles-deleuze-nietzsche-and-philosophy.pdf), translated by Hugh Tomlinson, preface pp. xi–xii; pp. 25–27, 40–41, 49–54, 175–176.
